facts.statement: Support systems for learning and development: linkage with performance appraisal (how far information flows from it to the learning and development system determines whether training stays developmental rather than a mechanical process); the human resource information system (HRIS), which stores on-the-job experience, placements and skills acquired through professional qualifications or training attended and serves as a database for training; and, most critical, the organisational culture: the superior who sends a subordinate for training, the HR functionary and top management are key players, and contradictory messages (a superior reluctant to nominate or relieve an employee, or top management not sanctioning budget or flexibility) wipe out the purpose of training. In one company the appraiser, at appraisal, acts as mentor and undertakes training of the appraisee in agreed areas, which becomes part of the appraiser's key result area for the next year. Rao (1988) lists beliefs that top management should reiterate: human resources are the most important assets; they can be developed to an unlimited extent; a healthy climate (openness, enthusiasm, trust, mutuality, collaboration) is essential; HRD can be planned and monitored to benefit both individual and organisation; employees are committed if they feel they belong, if basic and higher needs are met, and if they can discover and use their capabilities; every manager is responsible for development of subordinates and for a healthy climate; and higher-level managers should give more attention to HRD.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 215-216, Support Systems for Learning and Development

facts.statement: An attitude is a persistent tendency to feel and behave in a particular way towards some object (people, organisations, products, practices, ideology). Attitudes are not formed on rational, objective and complete information, so different people hold different attitudes to the same object. Attitudes tend to persist unless something is done to change them; they fall along a continuum from very favourable to very unfavourable; and they are directed at an object about which a person has perception, feelings and beliefs, often giving emotionally charged opinions and prejudices. An attitude has three components: emotional (feelings or affect: positive, neutral or negative), informational (beliefs and information about the object, which may not be empirically correct: a manager believing two weeks' training is enough when four are needed) and behavioural (the tendency to behave in a particular way towards the object).

Understanding attitudes matters because attitudes help predict work behaviour (a negative attitude to a changed work rule may show as absenteeism), help people adapt to their work environment, and are weighed in selecting and posting employees; imparting knowledge and skills is easier than changing a person's attitude, and a negatively oriented employee tends to find fault in every solution. Attitudes serve four functions: adjustment (helping people adjust to the work environment, for example a positive attitude to supervision after fair treatment), ego-defensive (protecting self-image, for example an older manager developing a negative attitude to a challenging younger subordinate), value-expression (expressing one's values, for example a manager who believes in the work ethic) and knowledge (supplying standards and frames of reference for making sense of the world, even where inaccurate).

Changing attitudes: the level of difficulty depends on how deep-rooted and emotionally charged the attitude is; the major barriers are prior commitment and lack (or distortion) of information. Ways to change attitudes: providing new information; the use of fear (low fear arousal is ignored, moderate fear arousal tends to change attitudes, and high fear arousal is rejected as too threatening and unbelievable, as with strongly graphic anticigarette messages); resolving discrepancies between attitude and behaviour (after choosing one of two job offers a person comes to feel positive about the one chosen and negative about the other); the influence of friends, peers and opinion leaders (leaders need to build interpersonal trust and present themselves as rational people interested in others' well-being); a manager who is friendly with and interested in the development of the employee, which also reveals learning needs; and co-opting dissatisfied people to help improve things (for example appointing a dissatisfied employee to the welfare committee).

A career is the sequence and variety of work roles, paid or unpaid, that individuals undertake throughout their lives; career development is a lifelong process of managing learning, work and transitions; a career path is a sequence of jobs that leads to short- and long-term career goals. After the initial excitement, individuals may become disillusioned if expected changes or advancements do not occur in time, causing frustration or alienation. Erikson divides life into eight stages, four in adulthood: adolescence (achieving ego identity), young adulthood (developing relationships and groups), adulthood (guiding the next generation, passing on knowledge and values) and maturity (achieving ego integrity by judging whether life has been meaningful). Levinson, studying the careers of 40 individuals, found that every five to seven years individuals pass through some career or personal crisis in a fairly predictable sequence of transitions corresponding to Erikson's adult stages.

Dalton, Thompson and Price (1977) describe four career roles: apprentice (the beginning of the career, routine work under a mentor, some dependency), colleague (an independent contribution, still in a subordinate role), mentor (complex functions: develops ideas, manages others, takes responsibility for subordinates' work) and sponsor (part of top management, needs a long-term perspective, defines the direction of the organisation or a major segment, chooses the right people who can support influencing). Driver (1985) lists career concepts: linear (planned upward movement within a profession), steady state (acquiring higher skills but not choosing to climb), transitory (shifting from job to job without necessarily acquiring excellence) and spiral (taking a new job, working hard, moving up, then moving on to a new type of work, geared to personal growth); a plateau is reaching a level above the start and staying there. Schein's three-dimensional career movements are vertical (up the hierarchy), circumferential (across divisions and functions) and radial (towards the centre of the organisation); a conical movement combines all three.

When movements across the horizontal plane (for example branches with different business focus), the controlling function and different levels of hierarchy are predetermined in a logical sequence, the organisation has a career path: a destination at a level or level of expertise, the distance, the crossroads and signboards (the criteria for eligibility to move). In a bank an individual might serve as apprentice in various branches, become a colleague, move to the controlling offices, then to larger branches, and as regional manager act as mentor. A defined path lets the organisation have competent people at all levels. Cautions: the organisational structure is pyramidal, fewer positions are available at higher levels, so the path does not ensure smooth movement for everyone; competitive conditions, supersession and bottlenecks create frustration, and people must be helped to accept that not everyone can reach the top.

Schein's career anchor is a personal sense of the type of work an individual wants to pursue and what it means to him or her: something that develops over time into a self-concept shaping personal identity, with three components (self-perceived talents and abilities, self-perceived motives and needs, and self-perceived attitudes and values). Schein found five anchors: technical/functional competence, managerial competence, security, creativity and autonomy. The external career refers to opportunities in the education system, society and organisations; the internal career to the individual's career anchors, that is the self-concept of what he or she is good at.

Career planning is a process of systematically matching career goals and individual capabilities with opportunities for their fulfilment (Schermerhorn, Hunt and Osborn). In an organisation it is an HRD subsystem that links manpower planning, job rotations, transfer, placement, training and performance appraisal; it is directed at structuring employees' aspirations for upward movement through the organisation and moderating unrealistic aspirations (Pareek and Rao, 1986), and does not mean management commits to promote anyone. The organisation should make the career planning policy explicit with performance benchmarks at critical stages; encourage employee growth and discourage superiors who suppress it; make clear that the career path is a facility for growth, not a right to advancement; make the career path (a sequence of job assignments, training requirements and promotion) known from the time of entry, with performance feedback; apply it uniformly without bias; and keep it flexible. Steps: define the career stages (roles) in relation to organisational levels; identify the core jobs at each level (comparable jobs form job families, and each individual should be assigned at least one job from the family); define transparent criteria, weightages and measurements for each successive level; and place the person in the next career role with training and counselling (the transition from colleague to mentor needs a developmental orientation, and from mentor to sponsor conceptual skills such as visioning, planning and creative problem solving).
facts.locator: Printed pp. 224-225, Career Path Planning: A System

facts.statement: Organisations increasingly have more than one career path: finance, personnel, marketing, planning, quality and information technology are now specialised functions that offer expert careers, so career plans can develop specific competencies, with core assignments of the specialist functions included in the general path. HR professionals must check that employees have a detailed understanding of the new job, the culture, the technology and the social atmosphere. Schein suggests career counselling workshops at different career stages so individuals can understand their career anchors in light of performance and introspection. In flatter organisations hierarchy is neither desired nor available and expertise in different areas matters, so Driver's spiral career concept becomes the ideal and the multiple-career concept more relevant.
facts.locator: Printed p. 226, Multiple Careers within Organisation

facts.statement: The self has a patent (external) part, such as identity and physical features, and an inner part, such as values, strengths and weaknesses; people are first identified by the patent self and later by the inner self. Self-development is developing a mature personality who can handle different tasks and situations with comparative ease, through ongoing self-improvement and discovery and use of one's potential. Organisational change stays superficial unless individuals' mindsets are altered (Pareek, 1994: "structures are modified and new reporting relationships are put down on paper but unless the individuals' mindsets are altered to this effect the change would be deceptive"), so organisations aiming to be learning organisations must make individuals the focal point of self-renewal. The factors that contribute to personal efficacy are motivation, self-awareness, proactive behaviour and action orientation (Pareek, 1997). The courseware discusses self-development at three levels: individual (motivational pattern, locus of control, power bases), interpersonal (interpersonal needs, transactional analysis) and group (being an effective member of the work group), together with emotional intelligence and morale.

Motivational pattern: individuals need to be aware of their life goals and need bases; people work for money, status, appreciation, work satisfaction, self-growth and so on, and the emphasis on a goal keeps changing, so HR policy must stay sensitive to changing needs. Locus of control (Leftcourt 1969, Levenson 1972): individuals with an internal locus of control believe that they can determine events and are geared to look for resources, anticipate events and take initiative; those with an external locus believe events are determined by outside forces such as other people, luck or destiny and wait for external forces. A person with an external locus can be reoriented towards internality by feedback that attributes success to his own efforts and ideas and not to the ease of the task or luck.

Power (Kotter, 1979) is a measure of a person's potential to get others to do what he or she wants and to avoid being forced to do what he or she does not want. Bases can be coercive (organisational position, punishment) or persuasive (expertise, competence, modelling). French and Raven (1960) identified five bases of power, which the courseware lists as coercive, legitimate, referent and expert and then expands with further types. The courseware describes: coercive power (threats and punishment); legitimate or position power (from the job description and delegation, belonging to the position rather than the person); reward power (the potential to reward worthy behaviour, including praise and recognition); referent power (respect leading followers to model the manager's behaviour); expert power (knowledge, skills, experience, credibility); knowledge power (similar, from knowledge of the job, people and organisation); reflected power (from proximity to a power source); charismatic power (emotional attraction from extraordinary characteristics); and emotional power (from personal relationships and emotional connection).

Schutz (1958) identified three basic interpersonal needs: inclusion, control and affection. Transactional analysis (Eric Berne; existential positions by Harris, 1969) treats a transaction as a stimulus and its response. Personality combines three ego states, Parent, Adult and Child. The Parent regulates behaviour and nurtures it (nurturing parent: understanding and caring; critical parent: judgemental); the Adult is logical, reasonable and unemotional, collecting and processing information, solving problems; the Child is concerned with creativity, curiosity, reactions and enjoyment (adopted child, natural child, little professor). Complementary transactions (Parent to Child and back, Adult to Adult) are desirable; crossed transactions (for example Parent to Child answered by Parent to Child) block communication and should be avoided. Harris's four life positions are: I am OK, you are OK; I am OK, you are not OK; I am not OK, you are OK; I am not OK, you are not OK. Pareek (1984) developed twelve influencing styles, six in the OK states and six in the not OK states.

A team is a group with a high degree of interdependence geared to achieving a goal or completing a task; group dynamics (a term from Kurt Lewin in the 1930s) concerns the internal nature of groups, how they form, their structure and processes, and how they function and affect individuals and the organisation. Members have two sets of roles: task roles (geared to the group's task) and maintenance roles (keeping the group cohesive, which has a long-term perspective: listening, respecting views, helping consensus). Consensus is often mistaken for compromise or majority rule; it means debating the pros and cons with respect for each member. The courseware lists the stages of group formation and behaviour as forming (awareness), storming (conflict), norming (cooperation), conforming (adjustment) and performing (productivity). Self-awareness can be helped by a SWOT analysis of oneself and by the Johari Window (Luft and Ingham, 1973), which crosses what is known or not known to self with what is known or not known to others: Arena or Open (known to both), Blind (known to others, not to self), Closed or Hidden (known to self, not to others) and Dark or Unknown (known to neither). Enlarging the Arena, by seeking feedback and by self-disclosure, improves effectiveness.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 234-235, Working in Teams and Self-awareness

facts.statement: Emotional intelligence is the capability to manage and control one's own emotions and to influence those of others; Goleman (1995) argues that IQ is not enough to predict success in life and that emotional intelligence, unlike IQ, grows through adulthood and can be learned. It has five components: self-awareness (recognising one's moods, emotions and drives and their effects on others: emotional awareness, self-assessment, self-confidence), self-regulation (controlling or redirecting disruptive impulses and moods: self-control, trustworthiness, conscientiousness, adaptability, innovation), self-motivation (passion to work for reasons beyond money or status: achievement drive, commitment, initiative, optimism), empathy (understanding others' emotional make-up: understanding and developing others, service orientation, leveraging diversity, political awareness) and social skills (managing relationships and building rapport: influence, communication, conflict management, leadership, change catalyst, building bonds, collaboration and cooperation, team capabilities).

Morale is the general mood of a person or group, whether confident, motivated and willing to perform tasks; high morale shows as confidence, cheerfulness, discipline and willingness to perform, and depends on motivation, rewards and recognition. Poor morale reduces productivity and revenue and raises staff turnover (the courseware cites a Sirota Consulting finding that low-morale companies' share prices rose 3 per cent against an industry average of 16 per cent). The morale boosters it lists include communicating often, welcoming ideas, keeping score and recognising top performers, inspecting what is expected, recognising employees, sharing success, putting employees front and centre (surveys, suggestion box, open-door policy), wellness and benefits, a personal touch from senior leadership, thank-you notes to the staff's families, a daily huddle, an open forum, having fun, showing charity, low-cost perks, dealing with a staff member whose negativity brings down the group, and measuring morale regularly through employee satisfaction. For negativity rooted in faulty information, solve the problem systematically with the affected employees, identify root causes, communicate at each step and involve people in the action plan.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 237-240, Morale and Employee Morale Boosters

facts.statement: The term talent management was coined by McKinsey and Company after a 1997 study (a 1998 paper by Chambers, Foulon, Handfield-Jones, Hankin and Michaels III). Talent can be seen as three Cs: competence (head: being able to do), commitment (hands and feet: action) and contribution (heart: doing it). Talent management is the anticipation of required human capital for an organisation and the planning to meet those needs; it covers acquiring, developing and retaining talent, and the courseware lists five key elements: attracting the right talent, onboarding, creating a talent pool, designing the talent career path and retaining talent; all are interdependent. The courseware argues that new-generation bank employees are more loyal to their careers than to their organisations, that employee turnover among highly talented employees will increase, and that they seek greater leisure, freedom at work, flexi-timing and work-life balance. Surveys of corporate talent management departments found its activities included succession planning, assessment, development and high-potential management, while compensation was not a function associated with it.

Succession planning is a process of identifying and developing new leaders who can replace old leaders when they leave, retire or die; it is a business strategy for passing leadership roles to another employee or group of employees, developing internal people with the potential to fill key leadership positions so that businesses keep running smoothly. It is distinguished from replacement planning, which is position-driven (naming specific back-up candidates for given senior positions, sometimes called the truck scenario) and which the courseware says research indicates has no substantial impact on outcomes; effective succession or talent-pool management builds a series of feeder groups through the leadership pipeline. Its objectives include identifying those with potential, providing critical development experiences, engaging leadership in developing high-potential leaders, and building a database for staffing decisions for key jobs; it improves commitment and retention, meets career development expectations and counters the rising difficulty and cost of external recruitment. It is an integral part of career planning and affects recruitment and selection, training and development and performance management. The courseware says Indian banks have developed senior management through sporadic, ad hoc exposures and quick promotion, which is inadequate, and calls for a comprehensive strategy supported by scientific competency assessment (assessment centre approach, 360-degree feedback) and for management development programmes for senior executives that focus on high-end soft skills.

payload.title: Support systems that make learning and development work
payload.core_explanation_md:
Training alone does not develop people. Three supports decide whether it does:

| Support | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Performance appraisal link** | Information from appraisals feeds learning needs; without the flow, training becomes a **mechanical** exercise |
| **HR information system (HRIS)** | Holds on-the-job experience, placements, skills and training attended: a **database for training** |
| **Organisational culture** | The most critical: superiors, HR and top management must **act** as if training matters |

A superior who hesitates to relieve a subordinate for training, or a top team that refuses budget and flexibility, wipes out the purpose of training. One company made the appraiser act as mentor and take on the appraisee's training in agreed areas, written into the appraiser's **key result area**.

**Beliefs top management should repeat** (Rao, as reported): people are the most important asset and can be developed without limit; a healthy climate (openness, enthusiasm, trust, mutuality, collaboration) is essential; commitment grows from belonging; every manager is responsible for developing subordinates; senior managers should give HRD more attention.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Contradictory signals are the usual failure: a policy that praises training while managers refuse to release staff.

self_check.prompt_text: Which of the three support systems does the courseware call the most critical?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The organisational culture, in which superiors, HR and top management show that training matters.

payload.title: What an attitude is, and its three components
payload.core_explanation_md:
An **attitude** is a **lasting disposition to feel and act in a certain way** towards something: a person, a bank, a product, a practice, an idea.

Three features: it **persists** unless something changes it; it can sit anywhere on a **scale** running from strongly favourable to strongly unfavourable; and it is **directed at an object** about which the person has perceptions, feelings and beliefs, which can make opinions emotionally charged.

Attitudes are **not** built on complete, objective information, which is why two people can hold different attitudes to the same thing.

| Component | Content | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Emotional** | Feelings: positive, neutral or negative | "I dislike touring" |
| **Informational** | Beliefs and information, perhaps inaccurate | A manager believes two weeks of training is enough when four are needed |
| **Behavioural** | The tendency to act | The manager allows only two weeks |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The informational component may rest on insufficient observation or opinion, which is why attitudes can be wrong yet still shape behaviour.

self_check.prompt_text: A manager believes a trainee needs only two weeks; four are really needed. Which component of the attitude is this?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The informational component (a belief that may not be correct).

payload.title: Why attitudes matter at work: four functions
payload.core_explanation_md:
Why study attitudes? They **predict behaviour** (a negative reaction to a new work rule may show up as absenteeism), help people **adapt** to the work environment, and are weighed when people are **selected and posted**. It is easier to impart skills than to change an attitude, and a negatively oriented employee tends to find fault in every solution.

Attitudes serve four functions:

| Function | What it does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Adjustment** | Helps people adjust to the work environment | Fair treatment by the boss produces a positive attitude to supervision |
| **Ego-defensive** | Protects self-image | An older manager whose decisions are challenged turns negative towards younger officers |
| **Value-expression** | Expresses one's values | A believer in the work ethic voices it to subordinates |
| **Knowledge** | Gives standards and frames of reference to make sense of events | A union officer's distrust makes everything management says "a pack of lies" |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The knowledge function shows that attitudes act as filters: they help us make sense of events even when the picture they give is inaccurate.

self_check.prompt_text: A manager who dislikes criticism from a younger subordinate develops a negative view of all younger officers. Which function?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Ego-defensive.

payload.title: Changing attitudes: barriers and methods
payload.core_explanation_md:
Attitudes can be changed, though with difficulty that depends on how deep-rooted and emotionally charged they are.

**Two main barriers:** **prior commitment** (the person is committed to a course of action) and **lack or distortion of information**.

**Ways to change:**

| Method | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| **New information** | May change beliefs and so the attitude |
| **Fear** | Moderate fear tends to work; **low** fear is ignored; **high** fear is rejected as too threatening |
| **Resolving attitude-behaviour discrepancy** | After choosing one of two jobs, people come to value the chosen one and devalue the other |
| **Friends, peers, opinion leaders** | Leaders who build trust and appear rational and caring shape followers |
| **A friendly, interested manager** | Learns the employee's motives and learning needs |
| **Co-opting** | Involve a dissatisfied person in improving things (for example the welfare committee) |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Co-opting works because, once people see how hard the problem is and how decisions are made, they are likely to change their view.

self_check.prompt_text: Which level of fear is most likely to change an attitude?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Moderate fear: low fear is ignored and high fear is rejected as too threatening.

payload.title: Careers: life stages, career roles and patterns
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **career** is the sequence and variety of work roles a person undertakes over life; **career development** is the lifelong business of handling learning, work and the moves between them; a **career path** is a series of jobs that leads towards short- and long-term goals. People who find that expected advancement is not coming on time become **disillusioned**, **frustrated** or **alienated**.

**Life stages:** Erikson (adult stages): adolescence (ego identity), young adulthood (relationships), adulthood (guiding the next generation), maturity (ego integrity). Levinson: a career or personal transition every five to seven years.

**Career roles** (Dalton, Thompson and Price):

| Role | Position |
| --- | --- |
| **Apprentice** | Routine work under a mentor; some dependency |
| **Colleague** | Independent contribution, still subordinate |
| **Mentor** | Complex functions; develops ideas, manages others, answerable for subordinates' work |
| **Sponsor** | Top management; long-term direction; chooses people to support |

**Career concepts** (Driver): **linear** (up the hierarchy), **steady state** (skills up, not rank), **transitory** (job to job), **spiral** (new type of work after moving up). A **plateau** means staying at a level.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Schein's three directions of movement: **vertical** (up), **circumferential** (across functions), **radial** (towards the centre).

self_check.prompt_text: Which career role is part of top management and chooses people to support its influence?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Sponsor.

payload.title: Career paths in an organisation, and career anchors
payload.core_explanation_md:
When movements across **branches and functions** and up through **levels** are laid down in a logical sequence, the organisation has a **career path**: a destination, the distance, the crossroads and the **signboards** (criteria for eligibility to move). In a bank: apprentice assignments in different branches, then a colleague role, a spell at controlling offices, larger branches, and as regional manager a mentor role.

**A caution:** the structure is a pyramid. Fewer posts exist at higher levels, so a path does not guarantee smooth movement. Competition, supersession and bottlenecks cause frustration; people must be helped to accept that not everyone reaches the top.

**Career anchors** (Schein) are a person's self-concept about the **work they want**, formed over time from self-perceived **talents and abilities**, **motives and needs**, and **attitudes and values**. Five anchors:

1. Technical/functional competence
2. Managerial competence
3. Security
4. Creativity
5. Autonomy
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The **internal career** is the individual's own self-concept of what he or she is good at (career anchors); the **external career** is the set of opportunities offered by education, society and organisations.

self_check.prompt_text: Name Schein's five career anchors.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Technical/functional competence, managerial competence, security, creativity, autonomy.

payload.title: Career path planning as an HR system
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Career planning** is a systematic matching of a person's career goals and capabilities to the opportunities available. In a bank it is an HRD subsystem linking manpower planning, job rotation, transfer, placement, training and appraisal. It structures employees' **aspirations** for upward movement and **moderates unrealistic ones**. It does **not** commit management to promote anyone: the path is a **facility for growth, not a right**.

**What the organisation should do:** state the policy and benchmarks; encourage growth and discourage superiors who suppress it; make the path **known from entry**, with performance feedback; apply it **without bias**; keep it **flexible**.

**Four steps to chalk out the path:**

1. **Define the career stages** (apprentice, colleague, mentor, sponsor) against organisational levels.
2. **Identify core jobs at each level**: comparable jobs form **job families**, and each person should hold at least one job from the family.
3. **Define transparent criteria** (weightages and measurement) for each next level.
4. **Place the person in the next role**, with training and counselling. Colleague-to-mentor needs a **developmental** outlook; mentor-to-sponsor needs **conceptual skills** (visioning, planning, creative problem solving).

**Multiple careers:** specialist functions (finance, HR, marketing, planning, quality, IT) offer expert careers; in **flatter organisations** the spiral concept becomes the ideal, and Schein recommends **career counselling workshops** to help people see their anchors.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Because top positions are few, a sensible career plan also moderates expectations and develops expertise across several areas.

self_check.prompt_text: Which two things should a transparent career criterion for the next level include?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The criteria (what is expected) and their weightages and measurement (how it is assessed).

payload.title: Self-development and personal efficacy
payload.core_explanation_md:
Everyone has a **patent self** (the external identity: appearance, role) and an **inner self** (values, strengths, weaknesses). First impressions are of the patent self; closeness reveals the inner one.

**Self-development** is the continuing effort to become a mature personality who can handle varied tasks with relative ease, by discovering and using one's potential.

Why it is the organisation's business: structures and reporting lines can be changed on paper, but unless people's **mindsets** change the change is only cosmetic (Pareek). Organisations that want to become learning organisations must make the individual the focal point of self-renewal.

**Personal efficacy** depends on four factors: **motivation, self-awareness, proactive behaviour and action orientation**.

The courseware covers self-development at three levels: **individual** (motivational pattern, locus of control, power bases), **interpersonal** (interpersonal needs, transactional analysis) and **group** (effective membership of a work group), plus **emotional intelligence** and **morale**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Individuals need to see that unless they change and develop, they will become a misfit as the environment changes.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the four factors that contribute to personal efficacy.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Motivation, self-awareness, proactive behaviour and action orientation.

payload.title: Motivational pattern, locus of control and power bases
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Motivational pattern.** People work for money, status, appreciation, satisfaction and self-growth; the mix keeps changing. Awareness of one's own goals and need bases helps people pick suitable development. HR policy must stay sensitive to changing needs.

**Locus of control** (Leftcourt; Levenson):

| Internal | External |
| --- | --- |
| "I can determine events" | "Luck, destiny, other people decide" |
| Takes initiative, looks for resources, anticipates | Waits for outside forces |

Someone with an external locus can be re-oriented through feedback that credits success to **their own** efforts and ideas, not luck or an easy task.

**Power** (Kotter: potential to get others to do what you want). French and Raven: coercive, legitimate, referent, expert (and reward). The courseware also describes:

| Power | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Coercive | Threat or punishment |
| Legitimate (position) | The position and delegation, not the person |
| Reward | Ability to reward, including praise |
| Referent | Respect; followers model the manager |
| Expert | Knowledge, skills, experience, credibility |
| Knowledge | Knowing the job, people and organisation |
| Reflected | Closeness to a power source |
| Charismatic | Emotional attraction of extraordinary characteristics |
| Emotional | Personal relationships and emotional bonds |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Awareness of the power one has, and how much more is needed, is part of being an effective leader. Power is also used in deciding who is rewarded and how.

self_check.prompt_text: A manager's power comes from her post in the organisation and would pass to anyone appointed to it. Which base?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Legitimate (position) power.

payload.title: Interpersonal needs and transactional analysis
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Interpersonal needs** (Schutz): **inclusion** (to be part of), **control** (to influence or be influenced) and **affection** (to be liked). Knowing your own pattern helps you see how you interact with colleagues, subordinates and superiors.

**Transactional analysis** (Eric Berne) studies a **transaction**: a stimulus and its response. A personality blends three **ego states**:

| Ego state | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| **Parent** | Regulates and nurtures; *nurturing* (caring) or *critical* (judgemental); right and wrong messages from elders |
| **Adult** | Logical, rational, unemotional; collects information; solves problems |
| **Child** | Natural impulses; creativity, curiosity, enjoyment (adapted child, natural child, little professor) |

**Complementary** transactions (Parent to Child and Child back to Parent; Adult to Adult) keep communication flowing. **Crossed** transactions (for example Parent to Child answered by Parent to Child) **block** it and should be avoided.

**Life positions** (Harris): I am OK, you are OK; I am OK, you are not OK; I am not OK, you are OK; I am not OK, you are not OK. Pareek developed twelve influencing styles, six in the OK states and six in the not OK states.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The aim is not to eliminate the Child (it carries creativity) but to be aware of which ego state is active and to choose behaviour that fits the situation.

payload.title: Working in teams, group stages and the Johari Window
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **team** is a group whose members are highly interdependent and aim at a goal. **Group dynamics** (Kurt Lewin, 1930s) studies how groups form, their structure and processes, and how they affect individuals and the organisation.

Members play two sets of roles: **task roles** (getting the job done) and **maintenance roles** (keeping the group cohesive: listening, respecting views). **Consensus** is not compromise or majority rule; it means debating the pros and cons with respect for each member.

**Stages** (as the courseware lists them): **forming** (awareness), **storming** (conflict), **norming** (cooperation), **conforming** (adjustment), **performing** (productivity).

**Self-awareness** can be helped by a **SWOT of oneself** and the **Johari Window** (Luft and Ingham):

| | Known to self | Not known to self |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Known to others** | **Arena** (open) | **Blind** |
| **Not known to others** | **Closed** (hidden) | **Dark** (unknown) |

To **enlarge the Arena**, seek feedback (reduces the Blind area) and disclose yourself (reduces the Closed area). A bigger Arena builds trust and effectiveness.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The usual textbook model of group stages is forming, storming, norming and performing; the courseware adds "conforming" between norming and performing.

self_check.prompt_text: A colleague tells you that you interrupt people, which you did not know. Which Johari window did this move into the Arena?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Blind window (known to others but not to self).

payload.title: Emotional intelligence and morale
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Emotional intelligence (EI)** is the capability to manage your own emotions and influence those of others. Goleman argues that IQ alone does not predict success; EI, unlike IQ, grows through adulthood and can be learned. Five components:

| Component | Meaning | Elements |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Self-awareness** | Recognising your moods, emotions, drives | Emotional awareness, self-assessment, self-confidence |
| **Self-regulation** | Controlling disruptive impulses; thinking before acting | Self-control, trustworthiness, conscientiousness, adaptability, innovation |
| **Self-motivation** | Passion beyond money or status | Achievement drive, commitment, initiative, optimism |
| **Empathy** | Understanding others' emotions | Understanding and developing others, service orientation, leveraging diversity, political awareness |
| **Social skills** | Managing relationships | Influence, communication, conflict management, leadership, change catalyst, building bonds, collaboration, team capabilities |

**Morale** is the general mood of a person or group: confident, motivated, willing. High morale shows as confidence, cheerfulness, discipline and willingness; it depends on motivation, rewards and recognition. **Poor morale** lowers productivity and revenue and raises turnover.

**Boosters** include communicating often, welcoming ideas, recognising and sharing success, surveys and open-door access, an open forum, thank-you notes, a daily huddle, and measuring morale regularly. For negativity from faulty information, solve the problem systematically with the people affected.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware cites a Sirota Consulting finding (low-morale companies' share prices rose 3 per cent against an industry average of 16 per cent) without further detail; treat it as illustrative.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the five components of emotional intelligence.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Self-awareness, self-regulation, self-motivation, empathy and social skills.

payload.title: Talent management: attract, develop, retain
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Talent** has three Cs: **competence** (the head: the ability to do the work), **commitment** (hands and feet: acting on it) and **contribution** (the heart: actually delivering).

**Talent management** is anticipating the human capital an organisation will need and planning to meet it. The term was coined by McKinsey and Company after a 1997 study. It covers **acquiring, developing and retaining** talent. The courseware lists five interdependent elements:

1. Attracting the right talent
2. Onboarding
3. Creating a talent pool
4. Designing the talent career path
5. Retaining talent

Why it matters in banks: demand for skilled people exceeds supply. The courseware argues that new-generation employees feel more loyalty to their **own careers than to the organisation**, that turnover among highly talented staff will rise, and that they seek leisure, freedom at work, flexi-time and work-life balance.

Surveys of corporate talent management departments found that their work covered **succession planning, assessment, development and the management of high-potential staff**; compensation was not part of it.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: If one element is out of step (for example attracting people without a career path for them), the whole structure weakens.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the three Cs of talent in the courseware?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Competence, commitment and contribution.

payload.title: Succession planning and replacement planning
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Succession planning** identifies and develops people who can take over from leaders who leave, retire or die. It is a business strategy for passing leadership roles on, by developing internal people with the potential to fill key positions.

| | Replacement planning | Succession (talent-pool) planning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Focus | Specific **back-up candidates** for given senior positions (the "truck scenario") | A **pipeline** of feeder groups through the leadership levels |
| Courseware view | Research suggests little effect on outcomes | The heart of effective succession planning |

**Objectives:** identify people with potential; give critical development experiences; engage leaders in developing high-potential staff; build a database for staffing key jobs.

**Benefits:** better commitment and retention; meets career development expectations; counters the rising cost and difficulty of external recruitment.

It is an integral part of **career planning** and touches recruitment, training and performance management.

**Banks:** the courseware finds Indian banks' approach (sporadic exposures, quick promotion to fill gaps) **inadequate**, and calls for a comprehensive strategy with **assessment centres and 360-degree feedback**, and management development programmes for senior executives focused on high-end **soft skills**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware quotes survey figures on small firms' lack of written succession plans and on how often firms pick the wrong people for manager roles; they illustrate the problem but were not independently checked.

self_check.prompt_text: How does replacement planning differ from succession planning?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Replacement planning names specific back-up candidates for specific positions; succession planning builds feeder groups across the whole leadership pipeline.

items.title: Support systems that make learning and development work
items.core_explanation_md:
Training alone does not develop people. Three supports decide whether it does:

| Support | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Performance appraisal link** | Information from appraisals feeds learning needs; without the flow, training becomes a **mechanical** exercise |
| **HR information system (HRIS)** | Holds on-the-job experience, placements, skills and training attended: a **database for training** |
| **Organisational culture** | The most critical: superiors, HR and top management must **act** as if training matters |

A superior who hesitates to relieve a subordinate for training, or a top team that refuses budget and flexibility, wipes out the purpose of training. One company made the appraiser act as mentor and take on the appraisee's training in agreed areas, written into the appraiser's **key result area**.

**Beliefs top management should repeat** (Rao, as reported): people are the most important asset and can be developed without limit; a healthy climate (openness, enthusiasm, trust, mutuality, collaboration) is essential; commitment grows from belonging; every manager is responsible for developing subordinates; senior managers should give HRD more attention.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Contradictory signals are the usual failure: a policy that praises training while managers refuse to release staff.

self_check.prompt_text: Which of the three support systems does the courseware call the most critical?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The organisational culture, in which superiors, HR and top management show that training matters.

items.title: What an attitude is, and its three components
items.core_explanation_md:
An **attitude** is a **lasting disposition to feel and act in a certain way** towards something: a person, a bank, a product, a practice, an idea.

Three features: it **persists** unless something changes it; it can sit anywhere on a **scale** running from strongly favourable to strongly unfavourable; and it is **directed at an object** about which the person has perceptions, feelings and beliefs, which can make opinions emotionally charged.

Attitudes are **not** built on complete, objective information, which is why two people can hold different attitudes to the same thing.

| Component | Content | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Emotional** | Feelings: positive, neutral or negative | "I dislike touring" |
| **Informational** | Beliefs and information, perhaps inaccurate | A manager believes two weeks of training is enough when four are needed |
| **Behavioural** | The tendency to act | The manager allows only two weeks |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The informational component may rest on insufficient observation or opinion, which is why attitudes can be wrong yet still shape behaviour.

self_check.prompt_text: A manager believes a trainee needs only two weeks; four are really needed. Which component of the attitude is this?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The informational component (a belief that may not be correct).

items.title: Why attitudes matter at work: four functions
items.core_explanation_md:
Why study attitudes? They **predict behaviour** (a negative reaction to a new work rule may show up as absenteeism), help people **adapt** to the work environment, and are weighed when people are **selected and posted**. It is easier to impart skills than to change an attitude, and a negatively oriented employee tends to find fault in every solution.

Attitudes serve four functions:

| Function | What it does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Adjustment** | Helps people adjust to the work environment | Fair treatment by the boss produces a positive attitude to supervision |
| **Ego-defensive** | Protects self-image | An older manager whose decisions are challenged turns negative towards younger officers |
| **Value-expression** | Expresses one's values | A believer in the work ethic voices it to subordinates |
| **Knowledge** | Gives standards and frames of reference to make sense of events | A union officer's distrust makes everything management says "a pack of lies" |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The knowledge function shows that attitudes act as filters: they help us make sense of events even when the picture they give is inaccurate.

self_check.prompt_text: A manager who dislikes criticism from a younger subordinate develops a negative view of all younger officers. Which function?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Ego-defensive.

items.title: Changing attitudes: barriers and methods
items.core_explanation_md:
Attitudes can be changed, though with difficulty that depends on how deep-rooted and emotionally charged they are.

**Two main barriers:** **prior commitment** (the person is committed to a course of action) and **lack or distortion of information**.

**Ways to change:**

| Method | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| **New information** | May change beliefs and so the attitude |
| **Fear** | Moderate fear tends to work; **low** fear is ignored; **high** fear is rejected as too threatening |
| **Resolving attitude-behaviour discrepancy** | After choosing one of two jobs, people come to value the chosen one and devalue the other |
| **Friends, peers, opinion leaders** | Leaders who build trust and appear rational and caring shape followers |
| **A friendly, interested manager** | Learns the employee's motives and learning needs |
| **Co-opting** | Involve a dissatisfied person in improving things (for example the welfare committee) |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Co-opting works because, once people see how hard the problem is and how decisions are made, they are likely to change their view.

self_check.prompt_text: Which level of fear is most likely to change an attitude?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Moderate fear: low fear is ignored and high fear is rejected as too threatening.

items.title: Careers: life stages, career roles and patterns
items.core_explanation_md:
A **career** is the sequence and variety of work roles a person undertakes over life; **career development** is the lifelong business of handling learning, work and the moves between them; a **career path** is a series of jobs that leads towards short- and long-term goals. People who find that expected advancement is not coming on time become **disillusioned**, **frustrated** or **alienated**.

**Life stages:** Erikson (adult stages): adolescence (ego identity), young adulthood (relationships), adulthood (guiding the next generation), maturity (ego integrity). Levinson: a career or personal transition every five to seven years.

**Career roles** (Dalton, Thompson and Price):

| Role | Position |
| --- | --- |
| **Apprentice** | Routine work under a mentor; some dependency |
| **Colleague** | Independent contribution, still subordinate |
| **Mentor** | Complex functions; develops ideas, manages others, answerable for subordinates' work |
| **Sponsor** | Top management; long-term direction; chooses people to support |

**Career concepts** (Driver): **linear** (up the hierarchy), **steady state** (skills up, not rank), **transitory** (job to job), **spiral** (new type of work after moving up). A **plateau** means staying at a level.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Schein's three directions of movement: **vertical** (up), **circumferential** (across functions), **radial** (towards the centre).

items.title: Career paths in an organisation, and career anchors
items.core_explanation_md:
When movements across **branches and functions** and up through **levels** are laid down in a logical sequence, the organisation has a **career path**: a destination, the distance, the crossroads and the **signboards** (criteria for eligibility to move). In a bank: apprentice assignments in different branches, then a colleague role, a spell at controlling offices, larger branches, and as regional manager a mentor role.

**A caution:** the structure is a pyramid. Fewer posts exist at higher levels, so a path does not guarantee smooth movement. Competition, supersession and bottlenecks cause frustration; people must be helped to accept that not everyone reaches the top.

**Career anchors** (Schein) are a person's self-concept about the **work they want**, formed over time from self-perceived **talents and abilities**, **motives and needs**, and **attitudes and values**. Five anchors:

1. Technical/functional competence
2. Managerial competence
3. Security
4. Creativity
5. Autonomy
items.expanded_explanation_md: The **internal career** is the individual's own self-concept of what he or she is good at (career anchors); the **external career** is the set of opportunities offered by education, society and organisations.

self_check.prompt_text: Name Schein's five career anchors.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Technical/functional competence, managerial competence, security, creativity, autonomy.

items.title: Career path planning as an HR system
items.core_explanation_md:
**Career planning** is a systematic matching of a person's career goals and capabilities to the opportunities available. In a bank it is an HRD subsystem linking manpower planning, job rotation, transfer, placement, training and appraisal. It structures employees' **aspirations** for upward movement and **moderates unrealistic ones**. It does **not** commit management to promote anyone: the path is a **facility for growth, not a right**.

**What the organisation should do:** state the policy and benchmarks; encourage growth and discourage superiors who suppress it; make the path **known from entry**, with performance feedback; apply it **without bias**; keep it **flexible**.

**Four steps to chalk out the path:**

1. **Define the career stages** (apprentice, colleague, mentor, sponsor) against organisational levels.
2. **Identify core jobs at each level**: comparable jobs form **job families**, and each person should hold at least one job from the family.
3. **Define transparent criteria** (weightages and measurement) for each next level.
4. **Place the person in the next role**, with training and counselling. Colleague-to-mentor needs a **developmental** outlook; mentor-to-sponsor needs **conceptual skills** (visioning, planning, creative problem solving).

**Multiple careers:** specialist functions (finance, HR, marketing, planning, quality, IT) offer expert careers; in **flatter organisations** the spiral concept becomes the ideal, and Schein recommends **career counselling workshops** to help people see their anchors.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Because top positions are few, a sensible career plan also moderates expectations and develops expertise across several areas.

self_check.prompt_text: Which two things should a transparent career criterion for the next level include?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The criteria (what is expected) and their weightages and measurement (how it is assessed).

items.title: Self-development and personal efficacy
items.core_explanation_md:
Everyone has a **patent self** (the external identity: appearance, role) and an **inner self** (values, strengths, weaknesses). First impressions are of the patent self; closeness reveals the inner one.

**Self-development** is the continuing effort to become a mature personality who can handle varied tasks with relative ease, by discovering and using one's potential.

Why it is the organisation's business: structures and reporting lines can be changed on paper, but unless people's **mindsets** change the change is only cosmetic (Pareek). Organisations that want to become learning organisations must make the individual the focal point of self-renewal.

**Personal efficacy** depends on four factors: **motivation, self-awareness, proactive behaviour and action orientation**.

The courseware covers self-development at three levels: **individual** (motivational pattern, locus of control, power bases), **interpersonal** (interpersonal needs, transactional analysis) and **group** (effective membership of a work group), plus **emotional intelligence** and **morale**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Individuals need to see that unless they change and develop, they will become a misfit as the environment changes.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the four factors that contribute to personal efficacy.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Motivation, self-awareness, proactive behaviour and action orientation.

items.title: Motivational pattern, locus of control and power bases
items.core_explanation_md:
**Motivational pattern.** People work for money, status, appreciation, satisfaction and self-growth; the mix keeps changing. Awareness of one's own goals and need bases helps people pick suitable development. HR policy must stay sensitive to changing needs.

**Locus of control** (Leftcourt; Levenson):

| Internal | External |
| --- | --- |
| "I can determine events" | "Luck, destiny, other people decide" |
| Takes initiative, looks for resources, anticipates | Waits for outside forces |

Someone with an external locus can be re-oriented through feedback that credits success to **their own** efforts and ideas, not luck or an easy task.

**Power** (Kotter: potential to get others to do what you want). French and Raven: coercive, legitimate, referent, expert (and reward). The courseware also describes:

| Power | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Coercive | Threat or punishment |
| Legitimate (position) | The position and delegation, not the person |
| Reward | Ability to reward, including praise |
| Referent | Respect; followers model the manager |
| Expert | Knowledge, skills, experience, credibility |
| Knowledge | Knowing the job, people and organisation |
| Reflected | Closeness to a power source |
| Charismatic | Emotional attraction of extraordinary characteristics |
| Emotional | Personal relationships and emotional bonds |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Awareness of the power one has, and how much more is needed, is part of being an effective leader. Power is also used in deciding who is rewarded and how.

self_check.prompt_text: A manager's power comes from her post in the organisation and would pass to anyone appointed to it. Which base?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Legitimate (position) power.

items.title: Interpersonal needs and transactional analysis
items.core_explanation_md:
**Interpersonal needs** (Schutz): **inclusion** (to be part of), **control** (to influence or be influenced) and **affection** (to be liked). Knowing your own pattern helps you see how you interact with colleagues, subordinates and superiors.

**Transactional analysis** (Eric Berne) studies a **transaction**: a stimulus and its response. A personality blends three **ego states**:

| Ego state | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| **Parent** | Regulates and nurtures; *nurturing* (caring) or *critical* (judgemental); right and wrong messages from elders |
| **Adult** | Logical, rational, unemotional; collects information; solves problems |
| **Child** | Natural impulses; creativity, curiosity, enjoyment (adapted child, natural child, little professor) |

**Complementary** transactions (Parent to Child and Child back to Parent; Adult to Adult) keep communication flowing. **Crossed** transactions (for example Parent to Child answered by Parent to Child) **block** it and should be avoided.

**Life positions** (Harris): I am OK, you are OK; I am OK, you are not OK; I am not OK, you are OK; I am not OK, you are not OK. Pareek developed twelve influencing styles, six in the OK states and six in the not OK states.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The aim is not to eliminate the Child (it carries creativity) but to be aware of which ego state is active and to choose behaviour that fits the situation.

self_check.prompt_text: A supervisor says "You people are always late" (Parent to Child) and the officer replies "And you never listen" (Parent to Child). What kind of transaction is it?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A crossed transaction: both speak from Parent to Child, so communication is blocked.

items.title: Working in teams, group stages and the Johari Window
items.core_explanation_md:
A **team** is a group whose members are highly interdependent and aim at a goal. **Group dynamics** (Kurt Lewin, 1930s) studies how groups form, their structure and processes, and how they affect individuals and the organisation.

Members play two sets of roles: **task roles** (getting the job done) and **maintenance roles** (keeping the group cohesive: listening, respecting views). **Consensus** is not compromise or majority rule; it means debating the pros and cons with respect for each member.

**Stages** (as the courseware lists them): **forming** (awareness), **storming** (conflict), **norming** (cooperation), **conforming** (adjustment), **performing** (productivity).

**Self-awareness** can be helped by a **SWOT of oneself** and the **Johari Window** (Luft and Ingham):

| | Known to self | Not known to self |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Known to others** | **Arena** (open) | **Blind** |
| **Not known to others** | **Closed** (hidden) | **Dark** (unknown) |

To **enlarge the Arena**, seek feedback (reduces the Blind area) and disclose yourself (reduces the Closed area). A bigger Arena builds trust and effectiveness.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The usual textbook model of group stages is forming, storming, norming and performing; the courseware adds "conforming" between norming and performing.

self_check.prompt_text: A colleague tells you that you interrupt people, which you did not know. Which Johari window did this move into the Arena?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Blind window (known to others but not to self).

items.title: Emotional intelligence and morale
items.core_explanation_md:
**Emotional intelligence (EI)** is the capability to manage your own emotions and influence those of others. Goleman argues that IQ alone does not predict success; EI, unlike IQ, grows through adulthood and can be learned. Five components:

| Component | Meaning | Elements |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Self-awareness** | Recognising your moods, emotions, drives | Emotional awareness, self-assessment, self-confidence |
| **Self-regulation** | Controlling disruptive impulses; thinking before acting | Self-control, trustworthiness, conscientiousness, adaptability, innovation |
| **Self-motivation** | Passion beyond money or status | Achievement drive, commitment, initiative, optimism |
| **Empathy** | Understanding others' emotions | Understanding and developing others, service orientation, leveraging diversity, political awareness |
| **Social skills** | Managing relationships | Influence, communication, conflict management, leadership, change catalyst, building bonds, collaboration, team capabilities |

**Morale** is the general mood of a person or group: confident, motivated, willing. High morale shows as confidence, cheerfulness, discipline and willingness; it depends on motivation, rewards and recognition. **Poor morale** lowers productivity and revenue and raises turnover.

**Boosters** include communicating often, welcoming ideas, recognising and sharing success, surveys and open-door access, an open forum, thank-you notes, a daily huddle, and measuring morale regularly. For negativity from faulty information, solve the problem systematically with the people affected.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware cites a Sirota Consulting finding (low-morale companies' share prices rose 3 per cent against an industry average of 16 per cent) without further detail; treat it as illustrative.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the five components of emotional intelligence.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Self-awareness, self-regulation, self-motivation, empathy and social skills.

items.title: Talent management: attract, develop, retain
items.core_explanation_md:
**Talent** has three Cs: **competence** (the head: the ability to do the work), **commitment** (hands and feet: acting on it) and **contribution** (the heart: actually delivering).

**Talent management** is anticipating the human capital an organisation will need and planning to meet it. The term was coined by McKinsey and Company after a 1997 study. It covers **acquiring, developing and retaining** talent. The courseware lists five interdependent elements:

1. Attracting the right talent
2. Onboarding
3. Creating a talent pool
4. Designing the talent career path
5. Retaining talent

Why it matters in banks: demand for skilled people exceeds supply. The courseware argues that new-generation employees feel more loyalty to their **own careers than to the organisation**, that turnover among highly talented staff will rise, and that they seek leisure, freedom at work, flexi-time and work-life balance.

Surveys of corporate talent management departments found that their work covered **succession planning, assessment, development and the management of high-potential staff**; compensation was not part of it.
items.expanded_explanation_md: If one element is out of step (for example attracting people without a career path for them), the whole structure weakens.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the three Cs of talent in the courseware?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Competence, commitment and contribution.

items.title: Succession planning and replacement planning
items.core_explanation_md:
**Succession planning** identifies and develops people who can take over from leaders who leave, retire or die. It is a business strategy for passing leadership roles on, by developing internal people with the potential to fill key positions.

| | Replacement planning | Succession (talent-pool) planning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Focus | Specific **back-up candidates** for given senior positions (the "truck scenario") | A **pipeline** of feeder groups through the leadership levels |
| Courseware view | Research suggests little effect on outcomes | The heart of effective succession planning |

**Objectives:** identify people with potential; give critical development experiences; engage leaders in developing high-potential staff; build a database for staffing key jobs.

**Benefits:** better commitment and retention; meets career development expectations; counters the rising cost and difficulty of external recruitment.

It is an integral part of **career planning** and touches recruitment, training and performance management.

**Banks:** the courseware finds Indian banks' approach (sporadic exposures, quick promotion to fill gaps) **inadequate**, and calls for a comprehensive strategy with **assessment centres and 360-degree feedback**, and management development programmes for senior executives focused on high-end **soft skills**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware quotes survey figures on small firms' lack of written succession plans and on how often firms pick the wrong people for manager roles; they illustrate the problem but were not independently checked.

self_check.prompt_text: How does replacement planning differ from succession planning?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Replacement planning names specific back-up candidates for specific positions; succession planning builds feeder groups across the whole leadership pipeline.
